One-dimensional label-box clustering and packing (a BoxArrange port)

Source: R/box-arrange.R
box_arrange.Rd

box_arrange() re-implements as pure functions the R5 reference class BoxArrange (plus its helpers Box and BoxCluster) from ComplexHeatmap:

Usage

box_arrange(start, end, range = range(c(start, end)))

Arguments

start, end

Numeric vectors giving the left and right end of each label box; they must have the same length. start need not be sorted.

range

Numeric vector of length 2, the range the boxes may occupy (e.g. c(0, 1)). Defaults to range(c(start, end)).

Value

A data.frame with columns start and end, in the same row order as the input (row i is the new position of the i-th input box).

Details

  1. sort the boxes by midpoint (the input need not be sorted);

  2. merge overlapping boxes (touching ends count) into clusters, in midpoint order;

  3. for each cluster use sum(width) as its span, lay the boxes end to end inside range (flatten), then iteratively merge the overlaps created by the edge shifts (merge);

  4. shift clusters that fall outside back into range (adjust_to_range) and merge once more;

  5. restore the original input order.

When the total width exceeds diff(range) (the boxes simply do not fit) it falls back to the proportional spread of ComplexHeatmap:::smartAlign2(): the first and last box stay glued to the ends and the rest are spread proportionally, so overlaps remain but every box stays inside range.

On feasible input the result matches the reference implementation (ComplexHeatmap:::smartAlign2(), the wrapper around BoxArrange) element by element within 1e-10. The differences are robustness and reproducibility improvements:

  • an empty input returns a zero-row data.frame; the reference throws subscript out of bounds;

  • boxes with identical midpoints are ordered deterministically (the reference uses rank(ties.method = "random"), which consumes random numbers and is not reproducible); results can only differ from the reference when exact ties occur;

  • a single box wider than range is centred; the reference returns -Inf.

The reference returns a matrix on the feasible branch and a data.frame on the infeasible one; this function always returns a data.frame.

See also

smart_align() for the circlize packing algorithm (which requires sorted input); smart_stack() for the multi-row label engine.

Examples

# two slightly overlapping boxes are packed end to end
box_arrange(c(0.10, 0.12), c(0.14, 0.16), c(0, 1))
#>   start  end
#> 1  0.09 0.13
#> 2  0.13 0.17

# unsorted input is fine: sorted by midpoint, returned in input order
box_arrange(c(0.60, 0.10, 0.30), c(0.64, 0.14, 0.34), c(0, 1))
#>   start  end
#> 1   0.6 0.64
#> 2   0.1 0.14
#> 3   0.3 0.34

# when the widths exceed the range it falls back to a proportional spread
box_arrange(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3), c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8), c(0, 1))
#>   start  end
#> 1  0.00 0.50
#> 2  0.25 0.75
#> 3  0.50 1.00
